notes.front: Who makes up the General Staff?
notes.back: Incident personnel organized by function, reporting to the IC or Unified Command: the Operations, Planning, Logistics and Finance/Administration Section Chiefs.
notes.explanation: This is the counterpart to Command Staff: General Staff runs the four functional Sections, rather than directly supporting command.
notes.example: Like four department heads, each running one major function, all reporting to the same IC.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

image.alt: Basic ICS organisation: the Incident Commander at the top; the Command Staff (Public Information Officer, Safety Officer, Liaison Officer) reporting to the Incident Commander; and the General Staff, four Sections side by side: Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Administration.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NIMS 2017, Fig. 3 and Table A-1, pp. 35, 92

notes.front: What is a Section, in ICS terms?
notes.back: The ICS organizational element responsible for a major functional area of incident management: Operations, Planning, Logistics or Finance/Administration.
notes.explanation: A Section is the organizational box; a Chief (next card) is the person who leads it.
notes.example: Like the Logistics Section: one organizational box responsible for all logistics work on the incident.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does the ICS title "Chief" mean?
notes.back: The ICS title for individuals responsible for managing a functional Section.
notes.explanation: Every General Staff member holds this one title, whichever of the four Sections they lead.
notes.example: Like the Operations Section Chief: the "Chief" leading the Operations Section specifically.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

image.alt: Ladder of ICS supervisory titles by organisational level: Section led by a Chief, Branch by a Director, Division or Group by a Supervisor, Unit by a Leader, and Strike Team or Task Force by a Leader.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NIMS 2017, Table A-1, p. 92

notes.front: What does the Operations Section do?
notes.back: Implements the tactical incident operations described in the IAP; it may include branches, divisions and/or groups.
notes.explanation: It is usually the largest and first-established Section, since it carries out the incident’s actual tactical work.
notes.example: Like the crews physically fighting a wildfire, organized under the Operations Section.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does the Planning Section do?
notes.back: Collects, evaluates and disseminates operational information, prepares and documents the IAP, and tracks the situation and resource status.
notes.explanation: It is the Section responsible for keeping the incident’s picture accurate and for producing the next IAP.
notes.example: Like the team compiling maps and status boards for tomorrow’s operational period.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does the Logistics Section do?
notes.back: Provides facilities, services and material support for the incident.
notes.explanation: It is the Section that keeps every other part of the incident supplied, housed and equipped.
notes.example: Like the team arranging food, radios and shelter for responders on a multi-day incident.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does the Finance/Administration Section do?
notes.back: Handles an incident’s administrative and financial considerations.
notes.explanation: It is established only when an incident needs incident-specific financial management, not automatically at every incident.
notes.example: Like the team tracking overtime costs and processing a contractor’s invoice during a multi-week response.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: In an expanding incident, which Section does the Incident Commander establish first?
notes.back: The Operations Section — the other Sections are established as needed to support it.
notes.explanation: Operations carries out the incident’s tactical work, so it is the first General Staff Section stood up as an incident grows.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 3, SM-p114

notes.front: Which Operations Section feature is about when it gets assigned, relative to other Sections?
notes.back: It is typically one of the first organizations assigned to the incident.
notes.explanation: These features describe how Operations tends to behave organizationally, separate from its list of tasks.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 6, SM-p118

notes.front: Which Operations Section feature describes how it develops, compared to the rest of ICS?
notes.back: It develops from the bottom up, rather than top-down.
notes.explanation: These features describe how Operations tends to behave organizationally, separate from its list of tasks.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 6, SM-p118

notes.front: Which Operations Section feature is about the amount of resources it holds?
notes.back: It has the most incident resources of any Section.
notes.explanation: These features describe how Operations tends to behave organizationally, separate from its list of tasks.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 6, SM-p118

notes.front: Which Operations Section feature is about extra organizational elements it may set up?
notes.back: It may have Staging Areas and other special organizations.
notes.explanation: These features describe how Operations tends to behave organizationally, separate from its list of tasks.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 6, SM-p118

notes.front: Which Planning Section activity is about producing the IAP itself?
notes.back: Preparing and documenting Incident Action Plans.
notes.explanation: The Planning Section’s work spans the whole incident record, not only writing the next IAP.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 8, SM-p120

notes.front: Which Planning Section activity is about keeping track of the incident's overall situation?
notes.back: Managing information and maintaining situational awareness for the incident.
notes.explanation: The Planning Section’s work spans the whole incident record, not only writing the next IAP.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 8, SM-p120

notes.front: Which Planning Section activity is about keeping track of resources assigned to the incident?
notes.back: Tracking resources assigned to the incident.
notes.explanation: The Planning Section’s work spans the whole incident record, not only writing the next IAP.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 8, SM-p120

notes.front: Which Planning Section activity is about keeping the incident's written records?
notes.back: Maintaining incident documentation.
notes.explanation: The Planning Section’s work spans the whole incident record, not only writing the next IAP.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 8, SM-p120

notes.front: Which Planning Section activity is about winding resources down at the end?
notes.back: Developing plans for demobilization.
notes.explanation: The Planning Section’s work spans the whole incident record, not only writing the next IAP.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 8, SM-p120

notes.front: Which Logistics activity is about ordering and accounting for supplies and equipment?
notes.back: Ordering, obtaining, maintaining and accounting for essential personnel, equipment and supplies.
notes.explanation: Logistics covers everything from supplies to medical care for responders themselves — not the affected public.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 10, SM-p122

notes.front: Which Logistics activity is about planning and providing communications resources?
notes.back: Providing communication planning and resources.
notes.explanation: Logistics covers everything from supplies to medical care for responders themselves — not the affected public.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 10, SM-p122

notes.front: Which Logistics activity is about feeding responders?
notes.back: Setting up food services for responders.
notes.explanation: Logistics covers everything from supplies to medical care for responders themselves — not the affected public.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 10, SM-p122

notes.front: Which Logistics activity is about setting up and maintaining incident facilities?
notes.back: Setting up and maintaining incident facilities.
notes.explanation: Logistics covers everything from supplies to medical care for responders themselves — not the affected public.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 10, SM-p122

notes.front: Which Logistics activity is about moving people and resources around the incident?
notes.back: Providing support transportation.
notes.explanation: Logistics covers everything from supplies to medical care for responders themselves — not the affected public.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 10, SM-p122

notes.front: Which Logistics activity is about medical care for incident personnel, not the public?
notes.back: Providing medical services to incident personnel.
notes.explanation: Logistics covers everything from supplies to medical care for responders themselves — not the affected public.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 10, SM-p122

notes.front: Which Finance/Administration activity is about negotiating and monitoring contracts?
notes.back: Contract negotiation and monitoring.
notes.explanation: These five activities are why Finance/Administration is set up for any incident needing incident-specific financial management.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 12, SM-p124

notes.front: Which Finance/Administration activity is about tracking personnel hours?
notes.back: Timekeeping.
notes.explanation: These five activities are why Finance/Administration is set up for any incident needing incident-specific financial management.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 12, SM-p124

notes.front: Which Finance/Administration activity is about analysing incident costs?
notes.back: Cost analysis.
notes.explanation: These five activities are why Finance/Administration is set up for any incident needing incident-specific financial management.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 12, SM-p124

notes.front: Which Finance/Administration activity is about compensating for injury or property damage?
notes.back: Compensation for injury or damage to property.
notes.explanation: These five activities are why Finance/Administration is set up for any incident needing incident-specific financial management.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 12, SM-p124

notes.front: Which Finance/Administration activity is about paperwork for reimbursement, e.g. under a mutual aid agreement?
notes.back: Documentation for reimbursement, e.g. under mutual aid agreements.
notes.explanation: These five activities are why Finance/Administration is set up for any incident needing incident-specific financial management.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 12, SM-p124

notes.front: If the Incident Commander does not establish a Logistics Section, who performs Logistics functions?
notes.back: The Incident Commander performs those functions directly, until a Section is established.
notes.explanation: This holds for any of the four Sections: whichever is not established, the IC performs its functions.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 9, SM-p121

notes.front: An IC has appointed four Section Chiefs, one for each functional Section, all reporting to the IC. What group do these Chiefs form together?
notes.back: The General Staff.
notes.explanation: This links the collective term to a concrete example of four Chiefs reporting to the IC.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 2, SM-p112

notes.front: Is "Operations" the name of a Section, or the title of the person leading it?
notes.back: A Section — the organizational element; the person leading it holds the title "Chief."
notes.explanation: This separates the organizational box (Section) from the person’s title (Chief).
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: The person leading the Planning Section is introduced at a briefing. What ICS title do they hold?
notes.back: Planning Section Chief — "Chief" is the title for anyone managing a functional Section.
notes.explanation: This applies the generic "Chief" title to a specific named Section.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A structure fire is rapidly growing and the IC decides to establish only one Section for now. Which Section should that be?
notes.back: The Operations Section — it is established first in an expanding incident.
notes.explanation: This applies the "Operations first" rule to a concrete, time-pressured scenario.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 3, SM-p114
notes.choices:
A) Operations
B) Finance/Administration
C) Whichever Section the first-arriving Chief happens to prefer
notes.choicesExplained: B: Finance/Administration is set up for financial matters, not urgent tactical needs. C: the order is fixed by the incident’s tactical need, not any Chief’s preference.

notes.front: Crews are physically fighting the fire, following tactics set out in the IAP. Which Section are they part of?
notes.back: The Operations Section.
notes.explanation: This connects the Section’s definition to the responders actually doing the tactical work.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: Does the Operations Section usually develop top-down, like the overall ICS organization, or bottom-up?
notes.back: Bottom-up — this is one of its distinguishing features, unlike the modular top-down growth of ICS overall.
notes.explanation: This tests a specific, easily-missed feature of Operations against the general Modular Organization rule.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 6, SM-p118

notes.front: A team is compiling maps, tracking resource status and drafting tomorrow’s IAP. Which Section is this?
notes.back: The Planning Section.
notes.explanation: This connects the Section’s definition to its most recognisable, concrete output.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: An incident is about to end, and a team is arranging the orderly release of resources back to their agencies. Which Planning Section activity is this?
notes.back: Developing plans for demobilization.
notes.explanation: This links a concrete end-of-incident task to one of the Planning Section’s five named activities.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 8, SM-p120

notes.front: A team is arranging shelter, food and medical support for responders on a multi-day wildfire. Which Section handles this?
notes.back: The Logistics Section.
notes.explanation: This connects the Section’s definition to its recognisable responder-support role.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: Does the Logistics Section arrange medical care for the affected public, or for incident personnel?
notes.back: Incident personnel — Logistics’ medical activity supports responders, not the public.
notes.explanation: This is a common confusion: Logistics medical support is for responders, while care for the public sits under Operations.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 10, SM-p122

notes.front: A contractor submits an invoice for equipment rented during the incident. Which Section handles processing it?
notes.back: The Finance/Administration Section.
notes.explanation: This links the Section’s definition to a concrete financial task.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A worker is injured on an incident and needs a compensation claim processed. Which Finance/Administration activity covers this?
notes.back: Compensation for injury or damage to property.
notes.explanation: This connects a concrete case to one of the five named Finance/Administration activities.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 12, SM-p124

notes.front: An incident is small enough that the IC has not established a Planning Section. Who tracks resources and prepares the IAP?
notes.back: The Incident Commander — performing the Planning functions directly until a Section is established.
notes.explanation: This applies the general "IC performs unestablished functions" rule to Planning specifically.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Visual 7, SM-p119
